newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Grain - Fall slows, pool cut looms.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Grain - Fall slows, pool cut looms.

text.p: Australia's grain price decline slowed during the past week as futures found some support at low prices and as the trade waited on the Australian Wheat Board (AWB) to cut its pool price estimate on Monday.
Guy Allen of GrainCorp described the market in cash and futures as both "fairly quiet in frustrated trade".
The frustration is over the AWB pool price, at A$190.00 a tonne for benchmark Australian Standard White (ASW).

The estimated pool price, for future world market sales, equates to about A$175.00 for present deliveries of ASW to Newcastle. This compares with Friday's ASW new crop cash market bids of A$142.00-A$146.00, with trades at about A$145.00.
The cash market had factored in a pool price decline of A$10.00-A$15.00 a tonne, Allen said.
Peter Howard of New England Agricultural Traders also said the trade was expecting a pool price cut of A$10.00 a tonne.
The market-slowing question has been whether the pool or cash prices are right. The answer will be in the price the AWB announces tonight.

Against this background, Howard saw the main action of the past week as parrying between demand for old crop and new crop grains as barley and some wheat began to come on the market from southern Queensland and northern New South Wales (NSW).
This also caused a tightening of freight rates and early logistical difficulties in moving material, he said.

Asked freight rates on a trucking run from northern NSW to Melbourne in Victoria had risen by about A$15.00 to A$60.00 a tonne. "They've got tremendous demand suddenly because the harvest is underway," Howard said.
Wheat was beginning to come off quickly from northern NSW, while the barley harvest was about 80 percent complete in the northern part of the state, he said.
While some harvested wheat from the western fringes of NSW was of poor quality, most wheat was very good with quite a lot of hard and prime hard, he said.
"So far so good," he said. "But we've got storms lurking."
Last week featured no big international news for Australian grain, apart from an AWB sale of 50,000 tonnes to Egypt.

Contacted by Reuters, a spokesman for the AWB confirmed negotiations had been held with Geneva-based wheat trader Romak, but declined to give further details. Romak is understood to be interested in purchasing a significant tonnage of wheat.
Over the past week, AWB indicator prices for ASW fell by A$3.00 and A$4.00 a tonne for Adelaide (A$142.00) and Melbourne (A$138.00) respectively, but rose by A$3.00 a tonne for Newcastle (A$141.00).
The AWB indicator price for Newcastle ASW bounced up by A$2.00 a tonne on Friday ahead of a stronger performance by wheat futures on the Sydney Futures Exchange (SFE).

SFE market leader January 1997 traded A$1.00 lower at A$147.50 on Friday, but brokers such as Phil Lindsay at Ord Minnett Jardine Fleming Futures Ltd took heart from buying support for the contract at around this level.
Most other futures contracts were steady to slightly down over the week.

A comparatively big day on the SFE on Friday saw 150 lots change hands, less than the record of 213 trades of September 26 this year but a sign that the present market level is beginning to activate buyers.
